title: Soldiers on the road
body: I am on the road to Damascus with our ten loads of linen. I travel with a caravan, a large group that goes together for safety. Soldiers of the Sultan are ahead of us, and the caravans are waiting. I can wait here with them, or go on by a quicker road that no one guards.

choices.label: Take the quicker road
choices.hint: It is faster, and no one guards it.

note: A caravan was a group that travelled together, to share water and guard each other. In 1326 Ibn Battuta rode with one from Cairo to Damascus in 21 to 23 days.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 67 and p. 80 n. 48; the caravan from Cairo to Damascus

title: A new toll on pepper
body: I am at Aydhab. The governor's men asked a new toll on our pepper, more than last year. I paid 60 of your money rather than wait a month. Now we sail.

choices.label: You should have argued
choices.hint: Ali may argue next time, and lose time.

choices.label: Complain to the court in Cairo
choices.hint: It costs money. It may help every house.

note: Ibn Battuta wrote that the money of Aydhab was shared by the sultan and the king of the Beja. One third went to the sultan.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 68 to 69; the revenue split of Aydhab

title: The wind for India
body: I am at Aden. The ships for India leave when the monsoon turns in summer, a wind that blows one way for months. If I go, I will not be home for a year and a half. If I stay, I can sell our goods here for less.

choices.label: Go to India
choices.hint: It is a long way and a big prize.

choices.label: Sell at Aden and come home
choices.hint: It is sooner, and for less.

note: A monsoon is a wind that blows one way for months and then turns. Ships crossed the Indian Ocean only when the wind was right, so the trade ran by its calendar.

sources.at: monsoon timing and the Red Sea trade
